macro_blurb: European equities are digesting a string of single-name stories rather than a unifying macro driver: Wacker Chemie is divesting its Siltronic stake, reshuffling the German chemicals and semiconductor wafer space, while BP removed chair Albert Manifold following bullying claims, adding governance noise to the UK energy sector. In autos, Ferrari shares fell after the unveiling of its first fully electric vehicle, a notable signal for the European luxury EV transition. Stateside, attention sits on mega-cap tech with renewed SpaceX–Tesla merger chatter tied to a potential Nasdaq listing, and on Apple ahead of a key event next month after its run to record highs. On the political side, Trump cancelled a Camp David cabinet meeting citing weather, and his administration is publicly split over Pope Leo's AI warning.
synthesis:
Today's screen is a US value-and-momentum sweep, full stop. All 10 picks are US-listed despite 992 names screened, with average Value at the 84.5th percentile and Momentum at 85.4 — but Quality sits at just 59.4 and Yield at 66.8. No single sector dominates: Financial Services and Healthcare contribute two each; the rest are singletons across Consumer Defensive, Basic Materials, Energy, Consumer Cyclical, Industrials and Technology. The composite range is narrow (72.6–85.1), which says the model is finding the same archetype repeatedly: cheap multiples paired with three-month outperformance, rather than any one cyclical thesis.

The thread connecting CF, APA, DAL and DVA is the cheap-and-running trade — trailing P/Es of 10.7x, 8.7x, 11.6x and 18.8x against sector medians of 32.4x, 16.6x, 29.9x and 25.6x, all with three-month returns above 19% against negative sector medians. In Financial Services, EG and CINF are the opposite stylistically — EG at 0.92x book with a 28.7% FCF yield reads as a distressed-value tell, while CINF at 9.6x earnings with D/E of 5.6 is the clean-balance-sheet version. Macro is unusually quiet on cross-currents; the European single-name noise around BP and Wacker doesn't touch this book.

The outlier is FSLR — the lone Technology name, carried by a 37% three-month return and US solar policy as the unpriceable swing factor. The conspicuous absence is mega-cap Tech: zero representation despite the SpaceX–Tesla and Apple headlines driving US tape. Utilities and Real Estate are also absent entirely. Watch two things over the next fortnight: the Apple event, which could pull momentum capital back toward mega-cap Tech and away from this value cohort, and any US solar policy headline that re-rates FSLR in either direction.
